reconcile.connective: Commentators read the Gospel "hate" as a Semitic idiom of comparative preference, so loving Christ more leaves the command to honor parents intact.

discrepancy.connective: The sharpest objection is pressed by E. P. Sanders, who argues that "let the dead bury their dead" required a follower to violate the binding duty to bury and honor a parent — a rare point where Jesus contravened the Mosaic law.

skeptic.name: E. P. Sanders
skeptic.attribution: E. P. Sanders (d. 2022), Jesus and Judaism (Philadelphia: Fortress, 1985), 252-255

excerpts.excerpt_text: And hate not - Matthew, Mat 10:37, expresses the true meaning of this word, when he says, He who loveth his father and mother More than me.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Directly defuses the central tension: 'hate' (Luke 14:26) is glossed as a Hebrew idiom meaning 'love less than me' (Matt 10:37), so it does not negate honoring parents.

excerpts.excerpt_text: not that proper hatred of any, or all of these, is enjoined by Christ; for this would be contrary to the laws of God, to the first principles of nature, to all humanity, to the light of nature, to reason and divine revelation: but that these are not to be preferred to Christ, or loved more than he, as it is explained in Mat 10:37 …
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: States plainly that literal hatred of parents is not commanded — it would contradict the law of God — and that the saying means only not preferring them above Christ, harmonizing with the honor command.

excerpts.excerpt_text: If the matter stands between God and him, as Theophylact saith: and therefore these words are not spoken simply, but by comparison.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Frames the 'hate' saying as comparative ('not simply, but by comparison'), engaging only when love of family conflicts with love of God — a distinct voice harmonizing the tension.

pd_work.resource: Adam Clarke, Commentary on the Bible (1832), note on Luke 14:26
pd_work.author: Adam Clarke
pd_work.note: Clarke treats this passage directly, reading the Gospel 'hate' as a Hebrew idiom for loving less (Matt 10:37; Gen 29:30-31), reconciling it with the command to honor parents.
